findings.title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and are cancelled when the request completes
findings.body: In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming apiserver request context. For server requests, the context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which happens immediately after the dual writer returns its response. The 10-second timeout therefore almost never gets to run: every legacy write races with request teardown and will frequently fail with context.Canceled. Since the failure is only recorded in a metric and never logged, mode 3 silently drops the 'safety' legacy writes it exists to perform, leaving legacy and unified storage permanently diverged with no signal. The goroutine context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (which preserves values like the logger and user) before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Delete records storage duration with the object name as the resource label
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's name in the position where every other call site in this file passes `options.Kind`. If the third argument is the metric's resource label (as all the kind-based call sites indicate), this creates a Prometheus series per deleted object name — unbounded cardinality that grows with every object — and breaks per-kind aggregation/alerting for the delete method. Use `options.Kind` here.

findings.title: Unified-storage failures are recorded as legacy metric errors (and vice versa in DeleteCollection)
findings.body: In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when `d.Storage` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — the failed unified-storage call is recorded as a legacy error and no storage-side failure is recorded at all. Conversely, in DeleteCollection's goroutine (line 166) the legacy delete-collection result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)`. These metrics misattribute failures to the wrong backend in both directions, which will mislead the dashboards/alerting used to judge whether it is safe to advance to mode 4. The Create/Update error paths should use `recordStorageDuration`, and the DeleteCollection goroutine should use `recordLegacyDuration`.

findings.title: Legacy goroutine reuses the request object that unified storage may have mutated and that is being serialized for the response
findings.body: The goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` with the same `runtime.Object` pointer that was just handed to `d.Storage.Create`. k8s-style stores mutate the object passed to Create/Update (setting UID, resourceVersion, generation, timestamps) and typically return that same pointer as `created`. If unified storage does that, the legacy goroutine and the HTTP handler then concurrently mutate and serialize the same object: the legacy store can overwrite unified's resourceVersion/UID on the object being written to the response — a data race and a potentially corrupted response body. Previously the legacy call was synchronous so mutation ordering was controlled; making it async requires passing `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the legacy call (same concern applies to the Update path reusing request-scoped objects).

findings.title: Unordered async legacy writes can leave legacy permanently stale (lost updates)
findings.body: Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no ordering guarantees. Two quick successive updates to the same object (or a create immediately followed by an update) can be applied to legacy out of order: the goroutine carrying the newer update may finish before the older one, which then overwrites legacy with stale data. Because legacy errors are only counted in a metric and never logged, nothing surfaces this divergence, and the legacy copy — the stated purpose of mode 3 ('just as a safe measure') — can silently remain at an old revision indefinitely. Legacy writes need per-object serialization (e.g. a single ordered worker/queue) and/or resourceVersion-based conflict handling.

findings.title: Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` should pass `log` — the logger that was just built with name/kind/method values. As written, anything downstream that uses `klog.FromContext(ctx)` (including the storage and legacy delete calls in this method) logs without the identifying fields, unlike every other method in this file which passes the enriched logger.

findings.title: Async legacy write failures are no longer logged anywhere
findings.body: In all four write methods the error from the async legacy call is only passed to `recordLegacyDuration`; the previous implementation logged it (e.g. `log.Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`). For a mode whose purpose is keeping legacy as a safety net, a failing safety net with no log entry makes diagnosis impossible — this would also have made the request-context cancellation bug visible in logs. Log the error with object identifiers inside each goroutine.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens
findings.body: The legacy expectations are registered on a testify mock that is shared between the legacy and unified mocks (both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`), and the tests return immediately after the dual-writer call without waiting for the legacy goroutine or calling AssertExpectations. Consequences: (a) the success cases pass even if the legacy call never runs — the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go fails nothing here; (b) because both backends share one mock, the Create error case registers only a 'legacy' expectation and it is actually `Storage.Create` that matches it, so the test's name and setup do not reflect what is exercised. Use separate mocks and wait/assert on the legacy invocation (e.g. require.Eventually) so each backend's call and ordering is genuinely checked.

findings.title: New mode-3 playlist subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous legacy writes and will be flaky
findings.body: `doPlaylistTests` performs k8s writes and then immediately reads through the legacy API (`getFromBothAPIs`, the 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' subtest, and the `/api/playlists` list comparisons) expecting both backends to agree. Under mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these cross-backend assertions race the legacy goroutine — they pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling (and fail outright whenever the legacy write is cancelled at request end, per the context bug in dualwriter_mode3.go). The two new mode-3 runs of this shared test need to poll for convergence on the legacy side (e.g. require.Eventually) or use relaxed expectations.
